description: Hydration is React's process of attaching event handlers to the server-rendered HTML DOM to make the application interactive. In Next.js App Router, only Client Components are hydrated — Server Components are never hydrated and have no client-side JavaScript. On the initial page load, Next.js serves pre-rendered HTML immediately, then the RSC Payload reconciles the component tree, and finally JavaScript hydrates Client Components. Hydration mismatches occur when the server-rendered HTML does not match what React produces during the first client render pass, causing React to either throw an error or re-render with warnings.

constraints.title: Server and Client Render Output Must Match on First Render
constraints.problem: If a Client Component renders different content on the server (during pre-rendering) versus the first client render (during hydration), a hydration mismatch error occurs.
constraints.whyItMatters: React compares the server-rendered HTML with the virtual DOM produced during hydration. Any difference causes React to either throw an error in development or silently re-render in production, discarding the server-rendered HTML and replacing it with a fully client-rendered version. This defeats the purpose of SSR, causes visual flashes (FOUC), and destroys performance metrics like LCP and CLS.
forbiddenPatterns: typeof window !== 'undefined' checks in render return paths
typeof window === 'undefined' conditional rendering
new Date() or Date.now() without suppression or client-only deferred rendering
Math.random() in render output
crypto.randomUUID() in render output without connection() guard
localStorage.getItem() in the render return
navigator.userAgent checks in render output
Rendering different content based on window.innerWidth in the initial render
Rendering content based on screen.width in the initial render
iOS/Safari auto-detection changing rendered HTML
CDN or proxy HTML minification that changes attribute order
Browser extensions injecting nodes into the DOM
allowedPatterns: useEffect with state update for client-only values (renders consistently on server, then updates on client)
suppressHydrationWarning={true} on elements with inevitably dynamic content (timestamps)
next/dynamic with ssr: false for components that cannot render consistently on the server
connection() from next/server before non-deterministic operations
Storing client-only values in state initialized after mount
productionRisks: Visual flash (FOUC) as server HTML is discarded and client re-renders
Degraded LCP and CLS Core Web Vital scores
Infinite re-render loops in edge cases
Console errors that confuse monitoring dashboards
SEO impact from inconsistent initial HTML
architectureImplications: Client Components must be designed to render the same output server-side and client-side on first render
Client-only state must be initialized to a server-safe default, then updated via useEffect
optimizationGuidance: Initialize all state with server-safe defaults (null, empty string, false) and populate client-specific values in useEffect
Use suppressHydrationWarning sparingly and only for truly unavoidable cases like formatted timestamps
quickFixes: Replace typeof window checks with a mounted state: const [mounted, setMounted] = useState(false); useEffect(() => setMounted(true), [])
Add suppressHydrationWarning={true} to elements with dynamic timestamps
Use next/dynamic with ssr: false for components that fundamentally cannot match server output
architectureSuggestions: Design Client Components to be 'isomorphic by default': the initial render should always produce the same output server and client
Treat client-specific personalization as a post-hydration concern: render a generic shell server-side, then update with user-specific data after mount

constraints.title: Only Client Components Are Hydrated
constraints.problem: Developers may expect Server Components to be hydrated (interactive) on the client, but Server Components produce no JavaScript bundle and are never hydrated.
constraints.whyItMatters: Server Components render only to the RSC Payload and static HTML. They have no associated JavaScript on the client. This is a feature, not a limitation, but misunderstanding it leads to attempts to add interactivity to Server Components, which silently fails. Event handlers on Server Components are no-ops.
forbiddenPatterns: Expecting onClick on a Server Component to work
Assuming useEffect runs in a Server Component
Assuming window is available after a Server Component 'renders' on the client
Using refs in Server Components to manipulate the DOM
allowedPatterns: Server Components produce HTML that is immediately visible without JavaScript
Hydration only occurs for Client Components within the page
Selective hydration: React prioritizes hydrating components the user interacts with first
productionRisks: Non-functional interactive elements if event handlers are placed on Server Components
Confusion in debugging when expected effects do not run
architectureImplications: The hydration boundary is precisely the 'use client' directive
Large pages with few Client Components hydrate very quickly because there is minimal JavaScript to process
Streaming + selective hydration means React can make individual Client Component islands interactive progressively
optimizationGuidance: Maximize Server Component surface area to minimize hydration work
Use Suspense boundaries to allow React to stream and selectively hydrate components as they arrive
architectureSuggestions: Design for 'minimal hydration surface': the less Client Component code there is, the faster and more reliable hydration becomes
Use streaming with Suspense so the browser can start hydrating arrived components while others are still loading

constraints.title: Avoid Disabling SSR for Core UI Components
constraints.problem: Using next/dynamic with ssr: false disables server-side pre-rendering for a component, producing an empty placeholder in the initial HTML that is filled in only after JavaScript loads.
constraints.whyItMatters: Disabling SSR for components causes a blank flicker during load, harms LCP, and removes the component's content from the initial HTML served to crawlers and users. It should only be used as a last resort for components that fundamentally cannot render server-side (browser-API-only widgets).
forbiddenPatterns: next/dynamic with ssr: false for components that could be made isomorphic
next/dynamic with ssr: false for above-the-fold content
next/dynamic with ssr: false for content that is important for SEO
Using ssr: false as a blanket solution for hydration mismatches instead of fixing the root cause
allowedPatterns: next/dynamic with ssr: false for widgets that are purely decorative and below the fold
next/dynamic with ssr: false for third-party scripts that only work in browser (maps, rich text editors)
next/dynamic with ssr: false as a last resort after all other hydration mismatch fixes are exhausted
productionRisks: Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS) from late-loading components
Missing content in search engine crawler HTML
architectureImplications: The default should always be server-rendered; ssr: false is an explicit override with known trade-offs
Loading skeletons should be provided via the loading prop when using dynamic() with ssr: false
optimizationGuidance: Fix hydration mismatches at their root (use the mounted pattern or suppressHydrationWarning) rather than disabling SSR
Reserve ssr: false for truly browser-only widgets
quickFixes: If using ssr: false for a mismatch, investigate the mismatch cause first: likely a typeof window check or Date.now() in render
architectureSuggestions: Establish a rule: ssr: false requires a code comment explaining why SSR is impossible for that component

invalid: const UserGreeting = dynamic(() => import('./greeting'), { ssr: false }) // Causes LCP degradation for important above-fold content
valid: const MapWidget = dynamic(() => import('./map'), { ssr: false, loading: () => <div className='map-skeleton' /> }) // Justified: map uses browser-only WebGL

constraints.title: Invalid HTML Nesting Causes Hydration Errors
constraints.problem:
Nesting HTML elements in ways that the HTML spec does not allow (e.g.,

inside

,

inside

, inside ,
constraints.whyItMatters: Browsers silently fix invalid HTML during parsing, moving or removing elements. React expects the DOM to match the server-rendered HTML exactly. The browser's auto-correction produces a DOM that differs from both the server HTML and React's expected tree, triggering hydration errors.
forbiddenPatterns: nested inside
nested inside
<a> nested inside <a>
<button> nested inside <button>
<form> nested inside <form>
<li> outside of <ul> or <ol>
<td> or <th> outside of <tr>
<tr> outside of <table>
Interactive elements nested inside other interactive elements
allowedPatterns: Using <span> instead of <div> for inline content within paragraphs
Using semantic HTML as per the HTML specification
productionRisks: Hydration errors in production causing React to fully re-render in the browser
Accessibility failures from broken semantic structure
architectureImplications: HTML validity is an architectural requirement for hydration correctness in SSR applications
optimizationGuidance: Enable eslint-plugin-jsx-a11y in CI to catch invalid nesting at development time
quickFixes: Replace nested <a> with a styled <span> or restructure the markup
